j.learned_fact: You are a little taller in the morning than at night because standing and sitting all day compresses you ('squished him down, just a little'), and you 'grow back' overnight.
j.thinking_skill: Proposing a causal explanation for a surprising measurement
j.notes: The first measurement happens 'on the wall' at the arena and the second at home, so the marks being compared are on different walls; the mechanism is only hinted at, never confirmed.

j.learned_fact: Bread dough grows bigger (rises) while it sits, and keeps rising in the oven; something inside it is at work.
j.thinking_skill: Inferring an unseen cause from an observed change
j.notes: Two unrelated halves (high singing, then dough) with a muddled timeline: the dough is first seen at snack time, then 'peeked at after music class', which already happened. Text is a touch young for age 6.

j.learned_fact: There are about 195 countries; Russia spans 11 time zones; Vatican City is the smallest country. FALSE detail: Russia's flag is described as 'a red flag with white stripes' (it is white, blue and red horizontal bands).
j.thinking_skill: Following a four-step plan and comparing extremes of size
j.notes: Facts are handed over as helper announcements rather than discovered; Theodore's line 'Bigger than my whole town, and smaller than my street' about Vatican City is self-contradictory, and the frost line is a random seasonal insert.

j.learned_fact: Two people pacing the same room get different step counts because their feet differ in size; a ruler works because 'every centimeter on a ruler is the same, everywhere' (standard units).
j.thinking_skill: Recognizing that a measurement disagreement comes from unequal units
j.notes: The teacher delivers the resolution rather than letting the boys work it out, and the frost-on-the-grass opening is decorative filler that goes nowhere.

j.learned_fact: Burrs stick to fur by tiny hooks catching loops, and Velcro works on the same hook-and-loop principle (true: Velcro was inspired by burrs).
j.thinking_skill: Analogical reasoning from nature to a device, then repeated testing to rule out chance
j.notes: Sentences run long for a third grader and the opening sorting-into-groups scene is a bolted-on second objective that never pays off.

j.learned_fact: Venice sits on more than a hundred small islands joined by bridges, has no cars, and moves mail, groceries and even ambulances by boat.
j.thinking_skill: Combining two known categories (boats, cities) and extrapolating what else must move by boat
j.notes: The reasoning stays light (mostly noticing), and the grandmother's island/bridge line is a small info-dump; 'mammal' joke works but is the only stretch word.

j.learned_fact: Sound travels faster through solid metal than through air, so a train can be heard through a rail before it is heard or seen (true: roughly 5000 m/s in steel vs 340 m/s in air).
j.thinking_skill: Forming a physical hypothesis from a sensory anomaly and transferring the idea to a new domain
j.notes: The vibration is heard through the railing of a footbridge over a creek, which is not the train track 'further down'; the story blurs bridge railing and train rail. 'New concept' and 'voluntarily' feel inserted.

j.learned_fact: Tapping a bottle gives a lower note the more water it holds, but blowing across it gives a higher note the more water it holds; the two patterns are reversed (accurate acoustics).
j.thinking_skill: Running controlled comparisons and tabulating results to reconcile contradictory observations
j.notes: Vocabulary misuse: 'he tried to hypothesize a full scale' (he tuned one, not hypothesized), and 'revolution' is shoehorned in via a pun; no mechanism (air column vs glass mass) is offered.

j.learned_fact: Water's boiling point depends on pressure: at high altitude (Cusco) it boils below 100 C so food cooks slowly, while a pressure cooker at about double pressure boils water near 120 C and cooks food much faster (both true).
j.thinking_skill: Extrapolating a relationship to its inverse case and testing the prediction experimentally
j.notes: 'Control' is misused: the carrots are the test subject, not a control (no comparison pot is cooked). The heat is killed the moment the valve hisses, so little time is actually spent at pressure.

j.learned_fact: A site that can email you your existing password is storing it in readable form; properly built sites store a scrambled (hashed) version they cannot reverse, which is why you must reset rather than retrieve a password, and why reused passwords are dangerous.
j.thinking_skill: Abductive inference: deducing a hidden system property from one observable behavior
j.notes: The antibody analogy and 'cordial expression' read as vocabulary being placed rather than arising; hashing is only gestured at rather than actually explained.

j.learned_fact: The greenhouse effect is natural and necessary, and the problem is its increased intensity, not its existence. FALSE: with -18 C without it and about 15 C with it, the difference is 33 degrees, not 'sixty three degrees' as stated.
j.thinking_skill: Exposing a hidden premise in an opponent's argument (natural implies more cannot be harmful)
j.notes: The central numeric fact is wrong by 30 degrees in a debate story whose point is winning on facts. 'Foible' is stretched to mean a debating habit; the text pitches more like grade 9-10 than 11.

j.learned_fact: Independent coin flips have no memory: after five heads the next flip is still 0.5, and runs of five or six in a hundred flips are expected, so a streak does not mean a win is 'due' (gambler's fallacy).
j.thinking_skill: Framing two rival hypotheses (bug vs chance) and designing a diagnostic test to discriminate them
j.notes: Vocabulary is visibly inserted ('despondent', 'implicated', 'reneged', 'rapport with the cursor'); 'implicated him personally' is a stretch. Printing the assigned probability only checks the declared p, not the RNG, so the test is weaker than the boys conclude.

j.learned_fact: A simulation only returns the assumptions built into it: if you encode that angry videos get more engagement, 'rage bait wins' is tautological, not evidence about the real world; demonstrating and matching reality are different questions.
j.thinking_skill: Epistemic self-critique: separating what a model demonstrates from what it assumes
j.notes: Contains a fenced code block (markup). The displayed six lines are valid Python, yet the plot hinges on a syntax error and a missing colon that is never shown; the pace is slow and the ending diffuse.

j.learned_fact: The first website went online in 1991 at CERN, and in 1993 CERN released the web royalty-free rather than licensing it (true). FALSE: print("hello grandpa") does not need a colon; 'You forgot the colon' would not fix a syntax error there.
j.thinking_skill: Holding two incommensurable value framings (ethical vs financial) of one decision at once
j.notes: The coding is wrong twice (colon on a print call; a for-loop 'running the whole time' before he ever wrote one), and 'Equivocal', dropped 'apropos of nothing', is a misuse: he means ambivalent. The web history arrives as a grandfather lecture.
